Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
43-year-old man with 5-day history of dry cough, rhinorrhea, and mild systemic aches; examination consistent with uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Dry, hacking cough and “cold” symptoms for ~5 days (started over the weekend).  
• Associated symptoms: Runny nose, myalgias, chills, occasional headache.  
  – Denies sputum production, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, wheeze, chest pain, or neck swelling.  
• Pertinent negatives: No fever reported; no worsening dyspnea.  
• Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (≈5–6 yrs); mild hypertension.  
• Medications: Metformin; Lisinopril; Paracetamol as needed.  
• Allergies: Not discussed.  
• Social / preventive: Secure location verified; no smoking, alcohol, or vaccination history discussed.

Examination:
• Visual (video): Mild pharyngeal erythema; tonsils not enlarged.  
• Neck: No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy (patient self-reported).  
• Chest: Not auscultated; patient denies wheeze or rattles.  
• Vitals: Home BP “within normal range” this morning; no other vitals provided.

Impression:
Likely viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold).  
  Supporting: Acute onset, dry cough + rhinorrhea, mild pharyngeal redness, systemic aches, absence of respiratory distress.  
Alternate considerations (less likely):  
  1. Influenza-like illness – systemic symptoms present but course currently mild and afebrile.  
  2. ACE-inhibitor–related cough – dry nature fits, but abrupt onset with concurrent viral features makes this unlikely.

Plan:
• Symptomatic relief: Over-the-counter combination remedies (Day Nurse/Night Nurse) acceptable with current medications.  
• Continue regular meds (metformin, lisinopril).  
• Red flag advice: Seek medical review if shortness of breath, wheeze, chest pain, hemoptysis, or if symptoms persist >3 weeks or significantly worsen.  
• No prescription, investigations, or referrals required at this time.  
• Routine diabetes and BP monitoring to continue.

Quality checks
● Missing elements: Allergies, smoking/alcohol status, temperature and full vitals, formal chest exam, vaccination status, planned follow-up timeframe.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but limited; objective vitals and physical exam (beyond pharynx) not performed, some conversational pauses.
